title: Prehospital Fluid Resuscitation for Patients With Suspected Sepsis: The PITSTOP-Fluids Factorial Randomized Clinical Trial
summary: This Ontario factorial trial randomized 1,686 adults; 1,646 contributed primary mortality outcomes. Median prehospital saline volumes were 1,500 versus 500 mL, but in-hospital death through day 90 was 149/830 (18.0%) versus 149/816 (18.3%): RR 0.98 (95% CI 0.80–1.20). Transport pulmonary edema occurred in 2.2% versus 1.0%.
findings: Pulmonary-edema checks followed each 250 mL; either group could stop fluids.
comparator: Saline for SBP <90, stopping at ≥100 mm Hg.
population: Adults with suspected infection, fever ≥38°C, SBP <100 mm Hg and IV access; four Ontario paramedic services.
limitations: Fever-selected suspected sepsis, saline-only regimens and unblinded clinicians limit generalizability. Small mortality differences remain possible; established vasopressor-dependent septic shock was not the studied population.
intervention: Up to 2 L IV saline regardless of subsequent SBP, until ED handover.
whyItMatters: Automatically giving more saline before handover did not improve survival; reassess perfusion and fluid tolerance. These findings do not establish equivalence or replace individualized septic-shock resuscitation.
evidenceNotes: Legal publisher full text reviewed, including methods/harms/limitations; supplements unreviewed. November 25 correction/later-evidence searches found originals/protocols, not a verified notice. Existing inpatient trials address different treatment stages.
primaryEndpoint: Death before hospital discharge, through day 90.
